title: Numerical Inequalities
summary: An inequality compares two quantities using <, >, ≤ or ≥ and usually has a whole interval of solutions rather than one value. This chapter covers the rules for manipulating inequalities, interval notation, linear, double, modulus, rational and simple quadratic inequalities, and their use in business and everyday word problems.

notes.heading: What an inequality is; interval notation
notes.html:
A numerical inequality is a statement that one quantity is less than (<), greater than (>), at most (≤) or at least (≥) another. 3 < 7 is a true inequality; x + 2 ≥ 5 is an inequality in a variable, true for all x ≥ 3.

The solution set of an inequality is the set of all values that make it true. It is usually written in interval notation:

InequalityIntervalEndpoints
a < x < b(a, b)open: both excluded
a ≤ x ≤ b[a, b]closed: both included
a ≤ x < b[a, b)a included, b excluded
x > a(a, ∞)∞ is always open
x ≤ b(−∞, b]b included

On a number line an included endpoint is shown by a filled dot and an excluded endpoint by a hollow dot.

notes.heading: Rules for working with inequalities
notes.html:
1. Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps the sign: a < b ⇒ a ± c < b ± c.
  2. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number keeps the sign: a < b, k > 0 ⇒ ka < kb.
  3. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the sign: a < b, k < 0 ⇒ ka > kb.
  4. Transitivity: a < b and b < c ⇒ a < c.
  5. Adding inequalities of the same direction: a < b and c < d ⇒ a + c < b + d (but they may not be subtracted).
  6. Reciprocals of positive numbers reverse the sign: 0 < a < b ⇒ 1/a > 1/b.
  7. Squares: if 0 ≤ a < b then a2 < b2; this fails for negative numbers (−3 < 2 but 9 > 4).

Modulus results (for a > 0): |x| < a ⇔ −a < x < a; |x| > a ⇔ x < −a or x > a. More generally |x − c| < a means x is within distance a of c.

A useful numerical inequality: for positive numbers a and b, AM ≥ GM, i.e. (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab), with equality only when a = b.

notes.heading: Method: solving different types of inequality
notes.html:
• Linear: expand, collect x-terms on one side, constants on the other, divide by the coefficient of x (reverse the sign if it is negative).
  • Double (combined): a < px + q < b — perform the same operation on all three parts.
  • System: solve each inequality separately and take the intersection (common part).
  • Modulus: convert |…| < a into a double inequality, and |…| > a into two separate inequalities joined by "or".
  • Rational (p(x)/q(x) compared with 0): bring everything to one side, never multiply by an expression whose sign is unknown, find the critical points (zeros of numerator and denominator), make a sign table, and exclude zeros of the denominator.
  • Quadratic: factorise, find the roots α < β; (x − α)(x − β) < 0 ⇔ α < x < β, and (x − α)(x − β) > 0 ⇔ x < α or x > β.

notes.heading: Worked Example 1 — linear and double inequalities
notes.html:
(a) Solve 3(x − 2) ≤ 5x + 4.

3x − 6 ≤ 5x + 4 ⇒ −6 − 4 ≤ 5x − 3x ⇒ −10 ≤ 2x ⇒ x ≥ −5. Solution: [−5, ∞).

(b) Solve −3 < (2x − 1)/3 ≤ 5.

Multiply all parts by 3 (positive): −9 < 2x − 1 ≤ 15.

Add 1: −8 < 2x ≤ 16. Divide by 2: −4 < x ≤ 8. Solution: (−4, 8].

(c) Solve 7 − 2x > 13. −2x > 6 ⇒ x < −3 (sign reversed on dividing by −2). Solution: (−∞, −3).

notes.heading: Worked Example 2 — modulus inequalities
notes.html:
(a) Solve |2x − 3| < 7.

−7 < 2x − 3 < 7 ⇒ −4 < 2x < 10 ⇒ −2 < x < 5. Solution: (−2, 5).

(b) Solve |x + 1| ≥ 4.

Either x + 1 ≥ 4, giving x ≥ 3, or x + 1 ≤ −4, giving x ≤ −5.

Solution: (−∞, −5] ∪ [3, ∞).

Interpretation: (a) says 2x is within 7 units of 3; (b) says x is at least 4 units away from −1.

notes.heading: Worked Example 3 — rational and quadratic inequalities
notes.html:
(a) Solve (x − 2)/(x + 3) ≥ 0.

Critical points: x = 2 (numerator zero) and x = −3 (denominator zero, must be excluded).

Intervalx − 2x + 3Quotient
x < −3−−+
−3 < x < 2−+−
x > 2+++

Quotient ≥ 0 for x < −3 or x ≥ 2 (x = 2 gives 0, allowed; x = −3 is not allowed). Solution: (−∞, −3) ∪ [2, ∞).

(b) Solve x2 − 5x + 6 < 0.

x2 − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). The product is negative only between the roots: 2 < x < 3, i.e. (2, 3).

notes.heading: Worked Example 4 — word problems
notes.html:
(a) A student scored 62 and 74 in two tests. What must she score in the third test (out of 100) to have an average of at least 70?

(62 + 74 + x)/3 ≥ 70 ⇒ 136 + x ≥ 210 ⇒ x ≥ 74. Since marks cannot exceed 100: 74 ≤ x ≤ 100.

(b) A firm's cost is C(x) = 26000 + 30x and revenue is R(x) = 43x, where x is the number of units sold. How many units must be sold to make a profit?

Profit when R(x) > C(x): 43x > 26000 + 30x ⇒ 13x > 26000 ⇒ x > 2000.

The firm must sell more than 2000 units, i.e. at least 2001 units.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Forgetting to reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
  • Cross-multiplying a rational inequality such as (x − 2)/(x + 3) ≥ 0 by (x + 3) — its sign is unknown. Use a sign table instead.
  • Including a zero of the denominator in the solution set.
  • Writing |x| > 4 as −4 > x > 4 (impossible). It must be "x < −4 or x > 4".
  • Squaring both sides when one side may be negative.
  • In word problems, ignoring natural restrictions such as "number of units is a whole number" or "marks ≤ 100".

keyTerms.definition: A statement comparing two quantities with <, >, ≤ or ≥.
One using < or >; the boundary value is not included.
One using ≤ or ≥; the boundary value is included.
The set of all values of the variable that satisfy the inequality.
[a, b] includes both endpoints; (a, b) excludes both.
Values where the numerator or denominator of an expression is zero; the sign can change only there.
|x| = x if x ≥ 0 and −x if x < 0; it measures distance from 0 on the number line.
Two or more inequalities to be satisfied together; its solution is the intersection of the individual solution sets.

formulas.name: Adding a constant
formulas.html: a < b ⇒ a + c < b + c

formulas.name: Multiplying by a negative number
formulas.html: a < b, k < 0 ⇒ ka > kb (sign reverses)

formulas.name: Modulus less than
formulas.html: |x − c| < a ⇔ c − a < x < c + a (a > 0)

formulas.name: Modulus greater than
formulas.html: |x − c| > a ⇔ x < c − a or x > c + a

formulas.name: Quadratic between roots
formulas.html: (x − α)(x − β) < 0, α < β ⇔ α < x < β

formulas.name: Quadratic outside roots
formulas.html: (x − α)(x − β) > 0, α < β ⇔ x < α or x > β

formulas.name: Profit condition
formulas.html: Profit ⇔ R(x) > C(x); break-even when R(x) = C(x)

mcqs.q: If a < b and c < 0, then
mcqs.explanation: Multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality, so ac > bc. (Likewise a/c > b/c.)
Divide by −4 and reverse the sign: x < −3.
−2 ≤ x − 3 ≤ 2 ⇒ 1 ≤ x ≤ 5; both ends included because of ≤.
|x| > 4 means x is more than 4 units from 0: x < −4 or x > 4.
2x < 10 ⇒ x < 5. Natural numbers less than 5: 1, 2, 3, 4 (0 is not natural, 5 is excluded).
Critical points −2 and 1. The quotient is negative only between them; x = −2 is excluded (denominator 0) and x = 1 gives 0, not < 0. So −2 < x < 1.

mcqs.q: The solution set of x<sup>2</sup> − 9 ≥ 0 is
mcqs.explanation: (x − 3)(x + 3) ≥ 0 holds outside or on the roots: x ≤ −3 or x ≥ 3.

mcqs.q: For a product, cost C(x) = 4500 + 25x and revenue R(x) = 40x. The least number of units that gives a profit is
mcqs.explanation: 40x > 4500 + 25x ⇒ 15x > 4500 ⇒ x > 300. At x = 300 there is break-even (no profit), so the least is 301.

mcqs.q: If 0 < a < b, which statement is always true?
mcqs.explanation: For positive numbers, taking reciprocals reverses the order: 1/a > 1/b. Also −a > −b and a<sup>2</sup> < b<sup>2</sup>.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): If −2x ≥ 6, then x ≤ −3.
Reason (R): When both sides of an inequality are divided by a negative number, the inequality sign is reversed.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Dividing −2x ≥ 6 by −2 and reversing gives x ≤ −3. A is true and follows from R.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): x2 > 4 implies x > 2.
Reason (R): If a > b > 0, then a2 > b2.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: x = −3 gives x<sup>2</sup> = 9 > 4 but x < 2, so A is false (the correct solution is x < −2 or x > 2). R is a true property of positive numbers.

questions.q: Write the inequality x ≥ −2 in interval notation.
questions.answerHtml: [−2, ∞) — square bracket because −2 is included; ∞ always takes a round bracket.

Critical points: x = −4 and x = 3.

Intervalx + 4x − 3Quotient
x < −4−−+
−4 < x < 3+−−
x > 3+++

Solution: (−∞, −4) ∪ (3, ∞). Neither endpoint is included (strict inequality; x = 3 makes the denominator zero).

questions.q: Solve the system 2x − 3 ≥ x − 7 and 3x + 2 < 2x + 9. How many integers satisfy it?
A medicine must be stored between 59 °F and 77 °F (inclusive). Using C = 5(F − 32)/9, find the range of temperature in °C.
questions.answerHtml:
59 ≤ F ≤ 77. Subtract 32: 27 ≤ F − 32 ≤ 45.

Multiply by 5/9 (positive, sign unchanged): 27 × 5/9 ≤ C ≤ 45 × 5/9 ⇒ 15 ≤ C ≤ 25.

The medicine must be stored between 15 °C and 25 °C.

questions.q: (a) Solve (2x − 1)/(x + 2) ≥ 1. (b) Solve x<sup>2</sup> − x − 12 ≤ 0. (c) Find the values of x satisfying both.
questions.answerHtml:
(a) (2x − 1)/(x + 2) − 1 ≥ 0 ⇒ (2x − 1 − x − 2)/(x + 2) ≥ 0 ⇒ (x − 3)/(x + 2) ≥ 0.

Critical points −2 and 3. Sign: positive for x < −2, negative for −2 < x < 3, positive for x > 3. Including x = 3 (value 0) and excluding x = −2: x ∈ (−∞, −2) ∪ [3, ∞).

(Note: cross-multiplying by x + 2 would have lost the part x < −2.)

(b) x2 − x − 12 = (x − 4)(x + 3) ≤ 0 ⇒ −3 ≤ x ≤ 4.

(c) Intersection of (a) and (b): [−3, −2) ∪ [3, 4].

questions.q:
Case study. A start-up assembles mobile phones. Its fixed cost is ₹1,80,000 per month, the variable cost is ₹1,200 per phone and each phone sells for ₹2,100. Its monthly capacity is 400 phones.
(i) Write the profit P(x) for x phones.
(ii) Find the least number of phones it must sell in a month to make a profit.
(iii) How many phones must it sell to earn a profit of at least ₹45,000, and what is the range of possible profit in that case?
